summary: Deep dive on KV cache eviction patterns, paging behavior under long-context sessions, and prefix reuse. Customer sees periodic latency spikes and throughput drops with synthetic long prompts; suspect eviction thresholds + prefix fragmentation. Discussed batching interplay, quantization effects, and VPC/on-prem constraints for private deployments. Agreed next steps: Redwood to reproduce eviction with Aperture sample, share traces and security docs, and schedule pilot kickoff pending POC approval.
topics: KV cache eviction heuristics and LRU vs generational policies
Paging & memory pressure on multi-tenant Dedicated instances
Quantization impact on cache size and eviction frequency
VPC / on-prem implications for debugging and kernel traces
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a deep dive on the kv cache behavior you reported. Luis and I are here from Redwood. can you kick off by summarizing what you saw?
[00:12] Rajiv Patel: yeah thanks, uh so over the last week we ran several 20k-50k token sessions and noticed intermittent latency spikes   tokens per second drops from ~1.2k to like 200 for short periods. throughput recovers but the sessions sometimes hit OOMs or paging.
[00:29] Luis Ortega: okay, and these are on your dedicated cluster or hosted?
[00:33] Samantha Lee: it's a dedicated pool we provisioned via Redwood Dedicated, on GCP in our VPC. we have about 8xA100-ish nodes, but we do also run a small on-prem proof-of-concept for compliance.
[00:46] Derek Huang: we tried lowering batch size to avoid OOMs but that increased p99 latency and didn't stop the periodic drops. We think cache eviction is thrashing.
[00:57] Luis Ortega: makes sense; common pattern is kv cache fills then eviction policy evicts prefixes that are still being referenced (prefix reuse). do you have long-lived sessions that reuse earlier prefixes?
[01:10] Rajiv Patel: yes   our apps often open a long chat context and then reference the same few hundred tokens repeatedly across turns, but also append new system instructions so the effective sequence grows.
[01:22] Maya Chen: are you using quantized model variants in prod? Q4 quantization can change key/value sizes and eviction footprint.
[01:29] Samantha Lee: we tested int8 quantized variants; they reduced memory but didn't fully solve the spikes. sometimes quantized runs had more frequent paging.
[01:38] Luis Ortega: that's expected; quantization reduces model weight memory but KV cache size scales with sequence length and kv dtype. if quantization changes kv dtype packing, you can end up with higher transient memory usage during generation paths.
[01:50] Rajiv Patel: can you elaborate on eviction policies? what does Redwood runtime use?
[01:55] Luis Ortega: we use an adaptive policy   per-worker LRU with heuristics for long-lived prefixes and a generational component to avoid immediate re-eviction of recently reused keys. but under memory pressure and high concurrency, eviction thresholds can be conservative and cause paging.
[02:10] Maya Chen: also we have auto-batching; batching helps throughput but increases simultaneous kv residency. high batch concurrency plus long contexts = more memory pressure.
[02:22] Samantha Lee: so there's a latency vs cost tradeoff   if we throttle batching we'll increase latency and cost. our SLA target is p99 < 450ms for typical shorter sessions but longer sessions can tolerate some p99 increases.
[02:35] Luis Ortega: right, one mitigation is prefix-aware caching: pin hot prefixes to avoid eviction during a session, or use sticky routing to a worker with warmed kv. we can instrument your workload to identify hot prefixes.
[02:48] Rajiv Patel: we attempted pinning but had issues when the worker crashed, the pinned state was lost and clients got inconsistent outputs.
[02:57] Maya Chen: that's why we recommend a small warm-up/replication factor for pinned entries; and use canary rollouts for changes. for on-prem, we can expose more deterministic placement for pinned keys.
[03:09] Derek Huang: you mentioned paging   what traces would you need to debug this?
[03:13] Luis Ortega: kernel-level vmstats, GPU memory allocator logs (cuda malloc failures), runtime eviction logs with timestamps, per-token latency traces, and a sample session reproducer. also the agent can collect kv cache occupancy over time.
[03:26] Samantha Lee: we can share partial logs; what about PII concerns? these sessions have user messages.
[03:31] Maya Chen: we accept redacted data; if needed use synthetic sessions that mimic token distribution. we'll also provide our SOC2, KMS integration docs so you can see retention and encryption controls.
[03:44] Rajiv Patel: ok. can you speak to prefix reuse fragmentation? how does that cause eviction?
[03:49] Luis Ortega: fragmentation happens when many prefixes differ slightly   like user adds minor edits   so cache sees many unique keys and cannot reuse earlier entries; the effective working set becomes much larger than anticipated. eviction then cycles through which causes p99 spikes when a recently referenced prefix was evicted.
[04:07] Samantha Lee: is there tooling to coalesce similar prefixes?
[04:10] Luis Ortega: on our side we have heuristics to normalize certain system tokens and dedupe near-identical prefixes, but it's workload dependent. we can run a profiler against your traces to estimate duplication rates.
[04:20] Rajiv Patel: about dedicated vs on-prem: we like dedicated for managed ops, but for compliance we may need on-prem and then debugging is harder because we don't have the Redwood control plane access.
[04:32] Maya Chen: for private deployments we provide an on-prem agent that can collect enhanced traces and upload them to your secure bucket or to Redwood with your consent. KMS/HSM integration keeps keys local.
[04:43] Derek Huang: do you support SAML SSO and RBAC for the console/agent?
[04:47] Maya Chen: yes, SSO via SAML/OIDC and RBAC; audit logs are available and can be exported. we'll include the security pack in the doc share.
[04:56] Samantha Lee: any quick tunables we can flip to reduce spikes now?
[04:59] Luis Ortega: short term: reduce max batch concurrency, increase evict threshold slightly, enable prefix pinning for known hot prefixes, and optionally lower kv compression level (paradoxically can reduce CPU overhead for small keys). we can provide a script to apply these on your Dedicated pool.
[05:18] Rajiv Patel: can you quantify impact? like expected p99 change vs cost delta?
[05:22] Maya Chen: we'll run a controlled repro and produce a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 before/after and estimated token cost delta. that's one of the next steps.
[05:32] Samantha Lee: one more thing   we saw a behavior where after a failover the new worker had empty cache and perf dropped; is there a recommended warmup strategy?
[05:41] Luis Ortega: yes, we recommend snapshotting frequently accessed prefixes and prewarming on new workers; we also support graceful failover that streams top-k prefixes to the new instance. depends on your tolerance for state replication.
[05:54] Derek Huang: for quantization mixes, any special considerations?
[05:58] Luis Ortega: mixed-precision can complicate cache layout; ensure consistent kv dtype across warmup and production runs. otherwise you may get alignment mismatches that increase memory.
[06:08] Rajiv Patel: timeline-wise, we want to have a POC by mid-October and decide on dedicated commit by EOY. can Redwood support a 2-week pilot on-prem?
[06:18] Maya Chen: yes, we can; we'll scope it after the repro results. pilot usually includes a small on-prem agent deployment and a Dedicated mirror for comparison.
[06:27] Samantha Lee: ok great. any notes on observability   dashboards we should look at?
[06:31] Luis Ortega: check per-worker kv occupancy over time, eviction events per second, per-token latency tracing, and GPU mem pressure metrics. We'll share a dashboard template.
[06:40] Rajiv Patel: thanks. can you also include recommended autoscaling rules? we saw nodes get saturated and then scale too slowly.
[06:47] Maya Chen: yes; we'll recommend reactive and predictive policies   reactive on queue depth and predictive on observed session starts + sequence length distribution.
[06:57] Derek Huang: competition question   we evaluated HF endpoints and Bedrock; they didn't give us the same low-latency guarantees and visibility.
[07:05] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include benchmark comparisons when we run your repro.
[07:12] Samantha Lee: ok let's recap next steps.
[07:15] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood runs repro (Luis) by 2026-10-06, Redwood shares security pack + SOC2 (Maya) by 2026-10-01, Aperture shares sample logs and autoscaler config by 2026-10-05, schedule pilot planning call for week of 2026-10-11.
[07:32] Rajiv Patel: yep that's right, thanks everyone.
[07:35] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up via email with artifacts and a calendar invite.
[07:40] (meeting ends)
